media:group.media:title: Arguing for Assemblage
media:group.media:description:
Within today's accelerated landscape of consumption and extraction, how does the technique of assemblage offer a different mode of inquiry for contemporary artists? This panel will explore assemblage-based sculpture—the use of found, mundane objects, combined in new and surprising ways—as a crucial tool for interrogating our entangled experiences of life under late capitalism. How do assemblage practices help reflect artistic experiences of migration and diaspora, political upheaval, and ecological crisis? How does the materiality of assemblage sculpture enact new performative modes of engagement in the contexts of its display—museums, galleries, artist-run spaces, and elsewhere? Does assemblage-based sculpture prompt a different, slower, mode of looking?
This panel welcomes art historical analyses of assemblage-based practices by contemporary and historical artists, alongside practice-based responses from artists who engage in this technique themselves.

entry.title: Asian Canadian Artists Participating in the Venice Biennale 2026

media:group.media:title: Asian Canadian Artists Participating in the Venice Biennale 2026
media:group.media:description:
This roundtable considers the significance of the especially strong presence of Asian Canadian artists at the 2026 Venice Biennale across national, invited, and affiliated platforms. Bringing artist Marigold Santos into conversation with art historian Asia Benedetti, and co-chairs Alice Ming Wai Jim and Marissa Largo, the session reflects on the practices and trajectories that converged in Venice and on the conditions under which Asian diasporic artists are exhibited, interpreted, and circulated. Participants will discuss artistic and curatorial experience, diasporic representation, national frameworks, and the broader stakes of visibility at this particular moment.
The roundtable asks what this convergence makes possible for Canadian, diasporic, and global art histories, while also attending to the interstices, institutional structures, and forms of relation that shape participation in the Biennale. The conversational format will include brief individual reflections followed by discussion among participants and with the audience.

entry.title: Dark Opacities Lab: Fugitive Planning in Practice

media:group.media:title: Dark Opacities Lab: Fugitive Planning in Practice
media:group.media:description:
This roundtable will introduce and explore the work of Dark Opacities Lab: a hub for BIPOC political and aesthetic study and strategy at Concordia University. The lab theorizes opacity through the triangulation of race, politics, and aesthetics: from theorizing around redaction to creative trans of color survival strategies; from historicizing visuality beginning with plantation slavery and interlocking colonialisms to envisioning abolitionist tools working against carceral technologies. Dark Opacities Lab engages with the evolving terms of opacity as a way to question the easy and extractive logics at play around race and representation, and to reorient around anticolonial struggles, global anti-racist social movements, and to centre the intersectional and the internationalist.
The roundtable will introduce the lab's three zines, its multi-year projects of "Nazar: A Theory of the Evil Eye" (2024-2027) and "No Pigs in Paradise" (2027-2030), as well as the work of toggling visibility as part of its fugitive practice in the university.

media:group.media:title: Toxic Museum
media:group.media:description:
Join us for a panel concerned with the manner in which the extraction of natural resources upholds the museum/art world: supplying funding for museums; creating art materials and exhibition infrastructure; and delivering the energy required for climate control to preserve artworks and artefacts
This panel encourages presentations that consider curatorial approaches, exhibition design, collections management, and art-making strategies that engage with extractivism or climate emergency; the breakdown of fossil-fuel-based materials in museum collections; toxic collections (however that is defined); and/or more sustainable or regenerative options for the sector.
Speakers
• Aaron Ambroso Three Gulf Coast Museums: Travel Reflections
• Nima Esmailpour Pocketing Heritage, Toxic Stewardship, and Unborrowed Reserves
• Allison Peacock Animating Asbestos: Musée Minero de Thetford and Exhibits of Toxic Histories
• Georgia Phillips-Amos Masters of Light
• Rojina Sabetiashraf Crude Reflections: Oil Pool and the Material Foundations of the Tehran Museum of Contemporary Art

entry.title: Queer Joy and Failure in Gender and Sexuality Research and Practice

media:group.media:title: Queer Joy and Failure in Gender and Sexuality Research and Practice
media:group.media:description:
Join us for the book launch of "Queer Joy and Failure in Gender and Sexuality Research and Practice", which offers a powerful intervention in gender and sexuality studies by theorizing queer joy not as merely pleasure, but as a radical practice shaped by failure, contradiction, grief, risk, and repair.
The book draws its argument from two major research projects: a study on queering sexuality education with over 80 in-service teachers in New Brunswick called SexualityNB and Pride/Swell+, a community-based participatory project involving over 300 2SLGBTQ+ people across Atlantic Canada. It investigates not only how queer joy circulates—through art, intimacy, activism, and chosen families—but also how it fails, revealing heartbreak, exclusion, and exhaustion within queer communities.
By examining failure as integral to theorizing queer joy in research and practice, the authors illuminate how breakdowns can become sites of solidarity, transformation, and worldmaking. The book advances queer joy studies, offering new ways to think about pedagogy, research ethics, and queer futurity.
About the Speakers:
• Casey Burkholder Casey Burkholder (she/her) is a queer femme Tier II Canada Research Chair in Social Justice in Youth and Child Studies and an associate professor at Concordia University. In choosing a research path at the intersection of resistance and activism, gender, sexuality, DIY media-making, art production, queer joy, and participatory archiving, Casey engages in research for social change through participatory visual approaches to local issues with 2SLGBTQ+ youth, adults, elders and teachers. She is the co-founder of the Fredericton Feminist Film Collective, and is the PI of Pride/Swell+ and SexualityNB.
• Melissa Keehn Melissa Keehn (she/her) is a femme lesbian and assistant professor at the University of New Brunswick. Before changing careers, she was an art and social studies teacher at a rural high school in New Brunswick. Her current research focuses on the relationships between gender, sexuality, and social change, particularly as they unfold within school contexts. A key strand of her work engages with sex education, exploring how curriculum, pedagogy, and teacher practice can either reinforce or disrupt dominant norms around sex, gender, and sexuality.
• Megan Hill Megan Hill (she/they) is a PhD candidate of education at Concordia University. Her doctoral research is about intergenerational knowledge exchange between elders and children within the 2SLGBTQIA+ community. She recently completed her master’s at Trent University, where she wrote an SSHRC-supported thesis titled Queer Crip Generativity. Megan is an active member of the JOY Lab and a research assistant on Pride/Swell+. In her spare time, Megan sometimes works at a queer youth summer camp developing accessible and joyful programming.

entry.title: Teaching with the COHDS Oral History Archives

media:group.media:title: Teaching with the COHDS Oral History Archives
media:group.media:description:
This roundtable panel centres on the collective experiences of teaching oral history at Concordia University by core affiliates and student affiliates of the Centre for Oral History and Digital Storytelling (COHDS). As educators and oral historians, we will discuss innovative approaches to working with COHDS’s archival collections and reflect on pedagogical strategies for engaging students with these resources. Drawing on our respective experiences of working with interviews from oral history collections such as: Montreal Life Stories (Refugee Youth Working Group, Rwanda Working Group, Haiti Working Group), Urban Changes in Little Burgundy, Pointe-Sainte-Charles: Balconville to Condoville, Urban History Laboratory among others, we are looking to share how the diversity of these oral history collections inform our pedagogy and work towards educating the next generation of oral historians.
A key facet of oral history practice is deep listening—a skill which must be cultivated in the classroom. For each panel participant, the COHDS’ archival collections have been a crucial space where students have had the opportunity to develop deep listening and understand the interviewer-interviewee dynamic in all its contexts: from listening to audio interviews, to reading a transcript, to analyzing the shared life stories and recollections of narrators. Through lively conversation and reflection, panelists Dr. Steven High, Dr. Barbara Lorenzkowski, Derek Xavier Garcia, Kelann Currie-Williams, and Lauren Laframboise will share the successes and challenges they have faced designing and incorporating interviews from COHDS’ collections into courses ranging from undergraduate to graduate levels.
Through this roundtable we will discuss: how can oral historians and educators design in-class activities that encourage a deep listening practice with archival materials? What are key approaches we can take to prepare students to engage ethically with interviews from the archives, particularly those from marginalized communities and difficult histories? How do we honour the ethical responsibilities to narrators who have donated these materials? How can educators engage with the resources available at COHDS and provide students with tools to engage with the multiplicity of interviews available online?

media:group.media:title: The Archive of the Future
media:group.media:description: Join us for a conversation with research librarians, archivists, and scholars reflecting on university-community research partnerships, imaginative ways of activating and mobilizing the archives, best practices of preserving large oral history collections, and what it means to archives by and for community. This conversation will speak to these challenges and the tensions that arise when community-grounded archival practice interacts with traditional archival institutions. Through conversation the panelists hope to offer best practices, insights, and share their experiences working to build an inclusionary archive for the future.

media:group.media:title: Learning How to Listen
media:group.media:description:
This conversation explores a central topic: How can oral historians listen closely, critically, and imaginatively to silences and emotion? How might speculative and creative practices preserve dimensions of testimony that exceed both language and transcription? What, finally, are the ethical challenges of documenting endangered oral traditions or stories of violence?
Over many years, the panelists have worked closely with Canadian World War veterans; women who participated in the Lebanese Civil War; Chinese-speaking immigrant women who experienced intimate partner violence; and the Mirasi community of Punjab. For all four panelists, relationality lies at the core of their commitment to non-extractivist research. Their research affords an extended contemplation of the principle of “Sharing Authority,” so foundational to our work at COHDS. In essence, panelists are reflecting on what we are doing to try and “make oral history a more democratic cultural practice.” (Zembrzycki, 2009)

media:group.media:title: Exploring Concordia’s Colonial Past #cu4thspace #concordia #montreal #truthandreconciliation
media:group.media:description:
The report “Exploring Concordia’s Colonial Past” was released last week as part of the National Day for Truth and Reconciliation at Concordia.

media:group.media:title: Storying Water
media:group.media:description:
Storying Water convenes Concordia research-creation scholars, including students and professors, who each work with water as an integral part of their practice, in conversation with Barbara Lorenzkowski. Through a series of short vignettes intended to animate the discussion to follow, each panelist will tell a story of how water informs their work.
Together, the presentations and discussion engage questions concerning careful listening, environmental awareness, flow, memory, embodiment, and sources and methods of storymaking.
About the speakers:
Gabriella Freeman “Raconte-moi le Ruisseau: An Oral History of the Urban Stream”
Gabriella Freeman is a textile artist, outdoor educator and grief counsellor starting their PhD at Concordia in Social and Cultural Analysis. Their experiences as a canoe guide in national parks and as an outdoor educator on the Lachine Canal have tuned them in to waterways as sites of meaning. Experiencing both "natural" and "wild" waterways, as well as “artificial” and “domesticated” urban waters has led them to interrogate such binaries and examine the ways in which humans relate to urban green and blue spaces. In their research, they approach the city through the urban wild, viewing its human residents as urban fauna. They recently published the oral history soundwalk Raconte-moi le Bois-des-Pères in the context of their undergraduate Honours Thesis (2025-2026), featuring resident storytellers who inhabit and relate to an urban woodland where water once flowed.
Laura Magnusson Laura Magnusson is a Montreal-based artist pursuing a PhD in Interdisciplinary Humanities at Concordia University. Working across video, drawing, sculpture, installation, and performance, she develops artistic strategies to communicate lived impacts of sexual violence and its institutional aftermaths. A trained scuba diver who has filmed underwater in Iceland and Mexico, Magnusson thinks, writes, and creates performative work at depth, exploring how underwater embodiment supports the processing and communication of traumatic knowledge. Magnusson has presented work in exhibitions, film festivals, and conferences across Canada and internationally with support from Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council (Doctoral Fellowship) and the Canada Council for the Arts. She served as a 2025-26 Concordia Public Scholar.
Liz Miller Documentary Encounters in the Hochelaga Archipelago
Elizabeth (Liz) Miller is a documentary filmmaker, educator, and Professor of Communication Studies at Concordia University in Montreal. She uses immersive and participatory documentary practices to connect personal experience with pressing social and environmental challenges. She has developed documentary projects such as The Shore Line,SwampScapes, and WasteScapes to engage audiences in timely issues such as climate change, water, waste, and environmental justice.Miller is co-author, with Steven High and Edward Little, of Going Public: The Art of Participatory Practice.
Polina Shubina Polina Shubina was born and raised on the shores of the Baltic Sea and has a background in theatre, puppetry, visual arts, and sailing. She is now pursuing her PhD in the Individualized program at Concordia University, with research-creation that explores sailing as a method and sailing ships as media for a transdisciplinary inquiry, community building, and outreach today. She has recently been working on several research-creation projects along the St. Lawrence River and delving into movement practice as a method of research.
Kathleen Vaughan Kathleen Vaughan (MFA, PhD) is an artist and academic with a trans-disciplinary orientation to questions of place and belonging, of "mattering" and matter. In studio and community projects, she balances her love for waters, green spaces, and skies with critical engagement, and often uses walking and mapping as method and form. Her work includes textile practices such as digital and hand embroidery, as well as photography, audio, video, and text. She chooses materials with a low environmental footprint, that ideally will biodegrade without adding plastic to our world. She is Professor of Art Education at Concordia University.
Barbara Lorenzkowski Barbara Lorenzkowski is an oral historian of childhood and youth whose work explores the ways in which global processes of migration, displacement, and violence have shaped small people’s lives in outsized ways. She recently published the co-edited anthology Small Stories of War: Children, Youth, and Conflict in Canada and Beyond (with Kristine Alexander and Andrew Burt, McGill-Queen’s University Press 2023) and is currently completing a FQRSC-funded book project on The Children’s War, a large-scale oral history project on children’s sensuous and emotional life-worlds in Atlantic Canada during the Second World War. Dr. Lorenzkowski served as the Lead Co-Director of COHDS between 2023 and 2026.

entry.title: Le récit du corps traumatisé avec Marie-Josée Gicali

media:group.media:title: Le récit du corps traumatisé avec Marie-Josée Gicali
media:group.media:description:
Ce projet est né de l’histoire personnelle de Marie-Josée en tant que rescapée du génocide contre les Tutsi au Rwanda. Une cicatrice sur son bras, souvenir d'une violence extrême, est devenue le point de départ d'une réflexion plus vaste sur les traces que le génocide a laissées sur les corps et les âmes des survivants. Blessée par balle lors des massacres de 1994, elle a longtemps porté cette cicatrice comme un stigmate. Aujourd'hui, elle est devenue un témoin, un support de mémoire et un point d'ancrage pour une démarche de recherche, de création et de transmission.
Ce panel proposera une réflexion sur les enjeux méthodologiques, éthiques et humains de cette recherche photographique et documentaire. Il abordera notamment les défis liés à la collecte de témoignages sur un sujet aussi sensible, ainsi que la posture de la chercheure, à la fois survivante, témoin et productrice de savoirs. Enfin, ce panel montre comment la recherche visuelle et documentaire peut contribuer à la transmission de la mémoire, à la lutte contre le négationnisme et à la promotion des droits humains.

entry.title: Memories of Migration with Andrew Jackson

media:group.media:title: Memories of Migration with Andrew Jackson
media:group.media:description:
Join us for a screening of three moving-image works, accompanied by an artist talk discussing these films alongside existing and forthcoming projects from Andrew Jackson's wider photographic and interdisciplinary practice. The programme comprises The Weight of Light (27 minutes), In Heart and Life and Longing, Part 2: Family Over Fame (20 minutes), and In Heart and Life and Longing, Part 3: Full Circle (19 minutes).
Across photography and moving image, Jackson's work considers family, migration, Black diasporic experience, memory and the political histories embedded within landscapes and everyday life. These films emerge from a sustained interest in the relationship between Jamaica, Britain and Canada, and in the ways that identity is formed through movement, aspiration, intimacy, loss and inheritance.
Moving between Quebec, Ghana, Jamaica and the United Kingdom, The Weight of Light considers migration, racialisation and the traces of colonial violence that landscapes can reveal, conceal and carry. It asks how land becomes a repository for histories that may no longer be immediately visible, but which continue to shape how places are understood, inhabited and remembered. The two films in the In Heart and Life and Longing series focus more closely on family, masculinity and the emotional weight of migration. Rather than treating their subjects as illustrations of wider social questions, the films make room for speech, silence, humour and contradiction. They resist simple narratives of success, failure or belonging.
The accompanying artist talk would place the films in dialogue with Jackson's wider practice, including Little Burgundy, The Sentence Stays With Me, a Canada Council for the Arts-funded post-documentary project on the enduring effects of incarceration after release; The Ground Beneath Us: Black Cartographies of Montreal, which examines Black spatial experience across Montréal. Together, the screening and talk would offer audiences an opportunity to engage with the moving-image works in depth, while also considering the research, ethical questions and lived encounters that shape my approach to photography and film.

media:group.media:title: The Political Power of Storytelling
media:group.media:description: Join us for presentations from Wendy Allen and Eva Crocker looing at intergenerational exchange through digital storytelling in Monteral and nostalgia and the queer utopic in Newfoundland. Moderated by Eric Craven, this session invites audience members to reflect on active aging, culture revivals, and nationalism through the lens of oral history.

media:group.media:title: Memories of the Border
media:group.media:description:
Join us for readings and screenings of selections from "Memories of the Border" followed by a discussion with those involved in the making of the series.
Since the summer of 2025, Montreal-based Solidarity Across Borders (SAB), a migrant justice network comprised of migrants and supporters, has been in collaboration with Concordia’s Feminist Media Studio (FMS) to create a community-led oral history project called “Memories of the Border”. Together, FMS and SAB work to create an interview testimonial series, giving voice to the experiences of undocumented migrants, tracing their journeys, their difficulties, and their hopes, while humanizing a reality that is too often invisible.
This project hopes to create an awareness-raising and advocacy tool for the regularization of undocumented migrants, provide a collective memory that bears witness to their presence and contribution to society, all while strengthening community solidarity by highlighting the voices of those whose experiences are often reduced to political debates and public discourse, rather than recognized through the complexity of their everyday lives.
Through this conversation, we hope to receive feedback on our work-in-progress and have a fruitful discussion about the power of community storytelling in contributing to political and social action, along with what it means, personally, to find empowerment in having one’s own story be heard, witnessed, and felt.

entry.title: Condensed Publishing: Preliminary Materials for Theory of the Young Micro Press with Kevin Lo

media:group.media:title: Condensed Publishing: Preliminary Materials for Theory of the Young Micro Press with Kevin Lo
media:group.media:description:
Part of the 9th edition of Volume MTL, the International Art Publishing Festival!
Assistant Professor Kevin Lo (Design and Computation Arts) will present in-process materials from the research-creation project Matter vs. Spirit, an investigation into the aesthetic, theoretical, material, and strategic relationships between publication practices and radical social movements. This event will also act as an informal inauguration of the micro-press with publications available for purchase.
